items.markingKey: 6 marks: credit each relevant point explained with NCERT evidence – Census 1881, high birth and death rates, 1921 year of great divide, low literacy and life expectancy, high IMR; occupational structure – 70–75% agriculture, regional variation; railways 1850, roads, waterways, posts and telegraph serving colonial interests.

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about the investment multiplier is correct?
items.answer: The paradox of thrift shows that an increase in the desire to save may reduce income and leave total saving unchanged.
items.markingKey: (c) The others are wrong: It works in both directions, including when investment falls. The multiplier is 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS. A higher MPS gives a smaller multiplier.
options: A higher MPS gives a larger multiplier.
The multiplier is equal to 1 ÷ MPC.
The paradox of thrift shows that an increase in the desire to save may reduce income and leave total saving unchanged.
The multiplier works only when investment increases.

The price of one unit of a foreign currency in terms of the domestic currency

items.stem: Explain the role of self-help groups in rural credit.
items.answer: Pool savings; small loans to members at reasonable rates; no collateral; women empowerment; reduces dependence on moneylenders; links with banks through microcredit.

items.stem: Explain the allocation, redistribution and stabilisation functions of the government budget.
items.answer: Allocation – provide public goods, non-rival and non-excludable; redistribution – taxes and transfers to reduce inequality; stabilisation – manage AD to reduce fluctuations in output, employment and prices.

items.stem: Explain the process of credit creation by commercial banks with a numerical example.
items.answer: Initial deposit e.g. ₹1,000 with reserve ratio 20%; ₹200 kept, ₹800 lent; ₹800 deposited and ₹640 lent; process continues; total deposits = 1,000 × 1/0.2 = ₹5,000.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: Initial deposit e.g. ₹1,000 with reserve ratio 20%; ₹200 kept, ₹800 lent; ₹800 deposited and ₹640 lent; process continues; total deposits = 1,000 × 1/0.2 = ₹5,000.

items.stem: "India joined the WTO as a founder member." Examine this statement with reference to privatisation and globalisation.
items.answer: The statement is valid. It wanted to be part of a rule-based trading system and get access to world markets.
items.markingKey: 3 marks: 1 for accepting or qualifying the statement, 1 for the reason (it wanted to be part of a rule-based trading system and get access to world markets.), 1 for supporting evidence from the chapter.

items.stem: 'China's one-child policy was both a success and a source of new problems.' Evaluate.
items.answer: Success – slowed population growth, higher per capita income; problems – ageing population, low sex ratio, fewer young workers; later relaxed.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: Success – slowed population growth, higher per capita income; problems – ageing population, low sex ratio, fewer young workers; later relaxed.

items.stem: 'APS can be negative, but MPS cannot.' Explain this statement.
items.answer: APS negative when saving negative (dissaving) at low income; MPS = ΔS/ΔY positive since saving rises with income; MPS lies between 0 and 1.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: APS negative when saving negative (dissaving) at low income; MPS = ΔS/ΔY positive since saving rises with income; MPS lies between 0 and 1.

items.stem: Explain the effect of a sharp rise in foreign investment inflows on the exchange rate of the rupee. How may the RBI respond?
items.answer: Supply of dollars rises; rupee appreciates (exchange rate falls); exports may become less competitive; RBI may buy dollars to limit appreciation and sterilise the money supply effect.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: Supply of dollars rises; rupee appreciates (exchange rate falls); exports may become less competitive; RBI may buy dollars to limit appreciation and sterilise the money supply effect.

items.stem: 'An increase in saving always slows the circular flow of income.' Examine.
items.answer: Saving is a leakage; if not matched by investment, aggregate demand and income fall; if saving is channelled through banks into investment, the flow is maintained; effect depends on planned investment.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: Saving is a leakage; if not matched by investment, aggregate demand and income fall; if saving is channelled through banks into investment, the flow is maintained; effect depends on planned investment.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"Railways changed the structure of the Indian economy by enabling long-distance travel and commercialisation of agriculture. Agriculture employed about 70 to 75 per cent of the workforce on the eve of independence. Infant mortality was very high on the eve of independence, about 218 per thousand. Before 1921, India was in the first stage of demographic transition with high birth and death rates."
(i) Explain the term 'occupational structure', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: 1921 is called the year of great divide. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "Most of India's workforce on the eve of independence was in manufacturing." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) The distribution of the workforce among the different industries and sectors. (ii) After it, death rates fell while birth rates remained high, marking India's entry into the second stage of demographic transition. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: About 70–75 per cent was in agriculture; manufacturing had about 10 per cent.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) The distribution of the workforce among the different industries and sectors. (ii) After it, death rates fell while birth rates remained high, marking India's entry into the second stage of demographic transition. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: About 70–75 per cent was in agriculture; manufacturing had about 10 per cent.

items.stem:
Study the extract below and answer the questions.
"The global issues of global warming and ozone depletion arise from environmental degradation. Pollution of air and water and the resulting diseases impose large costs on the economy. Earlier, the demand for environmental resources was less than their supply, but now it exceeds supply. When resource extraction exceeds regeneration, the environment fails to perform its life-sustaining function."
(i) Explain the term 'carrying capacity', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: The environment today faces a crisis of supply. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "Fossil fuels are renewable resources." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) The condition that resource extraction stays below the rate of regeneration and wastes stay within the assimilating capacity of the environment. (ii) Rising population and industrial production have made demand for resources and waste absorption exceed what the environment can supply. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: They are non-renewable resources that get exhausted with use.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) The condition that resource extraction stays below the rate of regeneration and wastes stay within the assimilating capacity of the environment. (ii) Rising population and industrial production have made demand for resources and waste absorption exceed what the environment can supply. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: They are non-renewable resources that get exhausted with use.

items.stem: Critically assess the economic achievements and failures of India during 1950–90.

"Pakistan followed a mixed economy model with both public and private sectors. China used special economic zones to attract foreign investment. India, Pakistan and China all started their development paths at about the same time. China adopted a command economy in which all critical sectors were owned and operated by the state."
(i) Explain the term 'commune system', which is related to the theme of the extract. (1)
(ii) Using the extract and your own knowledge, explain the following: China's growth accelerated after 1978. (1)
(iii) A student concludes: "China introduced reforms in 1991, along with India." Use your knowledge of the chapter to evaluate this conclusion. (2)
items.answer: (i) The system in China under which people collectively cultivated land. (ii) Reforms in agriculture, foreign trade and investment, and special economic zones attracted investment and raised productivity. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: China introduced reforms in 1978; India in 1991.
items.markingKey: 1+1+2 marks: (i) The system in China under which people collectively cultivated land. (ii) Reforms in agriculture, foreign trade and investment, and special economic zones attracted investment and raised productivity. (iii) The conclusion is wrong: China introduced reforms in 1978; India in 1991.

items.stem: 'A government running a fiscal deficit is passing a burden to future generations.' Critically discuss.
items.answer: Debt to be repaid from future taxes; interest burden; crowding out of private investment; counter-arguments – if borrowing finances capital assets or raises growth, future income rises; Ricardian view; size and use matter.

items.stem: 'The Great Depression changed the way economists looked at the economy.' Discuss, and assess the role that Keynesian ideas assign to the government.
items.answer: Pre-1929 belief in self-correcting markets; Depression showed long-lasting unemployment and fall in output; Keynes – deficient effective demand, need for public spending and policy; government and central bank as policy makers; assessment – role in short-run stabilisation, limits such as deficits and inflation; macroeconomics as a separate branch.

items.stem: Explain the process of money creation by commercial banks. What limits this process?
items.answer: Deposits, reserves and loans; rounds of lending and re-deposit; money multiplier = 1/LRR; numerical illustration; limits – reserve requirements (CRR, SLR), cash drain, excess reserves, demand for loans, RBI policy.
